headline_en: 34 Bangladeshis sent back from the United States
summary_en: Under the Trump administration's immigration policy the United States deported 34 Bangladeshis between 6 March and 21 April 2025 (46 days), according to immigration police at Dhaka's Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport. They had kept living in the US after losing immigration cases; some had been convicted in various cases. Foreign ministry officials said only people who lost legal battles are being returned, the ministry is told in advance, and more may be sent back.

facts.statement: The United States sent 34 Bangladeshis back to Bangladesh in the 46 days from 6 March 2025 to Monday 21 April 2025, under the immigration policy of President Donald Trump's administration.
facts.source_in_article: Immigration police, Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka

facts.statement: After Donald Trump took office for a second term, the United States began sending illegal (undocumented) immigrants back to their own countries from February 2025; the deportation of Bangladeshis is part of this.

According to police sources, the Bangladeshis deported from the US in March-April 2025 had continued living in the United States even after losing their immigration cases; those sent back also included people who had been convicted in various cases in the US.

Bangladesh foreign ministry officials said in April 2025 that only people who have lost their legal fight in the United States are being returned, and the Bangladesh foreign ministry is informed in advance about each person being returned.
facts.source_in_article: Officials of the Bangladesh Ministry of Foreign Affairs

facts.statement: Bangladesh foreign ministry officials said in April 2025 that more Bangladeshis may be sent back from the United States in the coming days.
facts.source_in_article: Officials of the Bangladesh Ministry of Foreign Affairs

Among economic points it says remittance in March 2025 exceeded USD 3 billion, with USD 329 crore through legal banking channels, 64.7% more than March 2024, and that remittance and exports have kept the government in a good position. headline_en: Qatar migrant returns home in the morning, dies under a train in the evening
summary_en: Abul Basar (48) of Senbagh, Noakhali, who had lived in Qatar for 24 years, returned to Dhaka on 7 April 2025 without telling his family after finding no work in Qatar and suffering depression. After an argument by phone with his wife, who had told him not to come back, he was killed by a train at Chowmuhani railway station that evening; railway police suspect suicide over a family quarrel.

facts.statement: Qatar returnee Abul Basar (48), of Uttar Sahapur village, Kabilpur union, Senbagh upazila, Noakhali, arrived in Dhaka on the morning of Monday 7 April 2025 and died the same evening around 7:30 pm when he lay his head on the rail line at Chowmuhani railway station, Begumganj upazila, Noakhali, and was hit by a train coming from Laksam, Cumilla.

Abul Basar, who had been in Qatar for 24 years, came home in January 2025 for his only daughter's wedding and went back to Qatar, but found no work there and suffered from depression (hotasha), according to his cousin.

When Abul Basar told his wife he had decided to return from Qatar, she told him not to; he then returned without telling anyone in the family, and after a phone argument with her said 'if I don't come, my corpse will go home.'

Chowmuhani railway police outpost recovered Abul Basar's body and sent it to the Noakhali General Hospital morgue for autopsy; police said they initially believe he committed suicide over a family quarrel and an unnatural death case would be filed.
facts.source_in_article: SI Pradip Kumar Majumder, officer in charge, Chowmuhani railway police outpost

people_cases.what_happened: Lived in Qatar 24 years with two brothers there; returned Jan 2025 for daughter's wedding, went back, found no work, became depressed, returned unannounced on 7 April 2025 against his wife's wishes.
people_cases.outcome: Died under a train at Chowmuhani station the same evening; police suspect suicide; unnatural death case to be filed.

headline_en: Joining the LDC list is optional, leaving it is predetermined (interview)
summary_en: Interview with CPD's Mustafizur Rahman on the economy under the interim government, money laundering and LDC graduation on 24 November 2026. On migration-related points he says remittance inflows are the highest ever, credits migrant workers and the interim government's clean image among expatriates for moving people away from hundi, and describes how hundi and a 'vicious circle' around remittance moved laundered money to Dubai, Singapore, Malaysia, the UK, US and Canada. He also cites gold from the UAE far exceeding declared imports.

facts.statement: Mustafizur Rahman of CPD said in March 2025 that remittance (probashi ay) was coming in well, and that the highest remittance of all time was being received; he said migrant workers deserve major credit for this.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafizur Rahman, distinguished fellow, Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), interview with Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Mustafizur Rahman said in March 2025 that the interim government made an important contribution to moving expatriates away from hundi-hawala by stressing that money sent through legal channels serves the country, while through hundi-hawala corrupt people, tax defaulters, loan defaulters and some politicians launder money abroad; he said the government built a clean image among expatriates.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafizur Rahman, distinguished fellow, Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), interview with Prothom Alo

facts.statement: According to the white paper committee on the economy (cited by Mustafizur Rahman), about USD 16 billion was laundered out of Bangladesh during the Hasina government's tenure, about 5% of GDP.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafizur Rahman, distinguished fellow, Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), interview with Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Mustafizur Rahman said a vicious circle formed around hundi-hawala and remittance which laundered money from Bangladesh to Dubai, Singapore, Malaysia, the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada, where it was kept in bank accounts and used to buy property; many layers were created between sender and receiver so the paper trail is hard to establish.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafizur Rahman, distinguished fellow, Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), interview with Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Citing Prothom Alo, Mustafizur Rahman said gold worth about USD 366.64 crore (about BDT 40,000 crore) came from the United Arab Emirates to Bangladesh in 10 years, but only USD 82 lakh of gold imports were shown in Bangladesh, indicating a nexus between money launderers and gold smugglers.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafizur Rahman, distinguished fellow, Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), interview with Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Mustafizur Rahman said in March 2025 that the interim government had clearly decided Bangladesh will graduate from the least developed country (LDC) list on 24 November 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafizur Rahman, distinguished fellow, Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), interview with Prothom Alo

headline_en: Immigration problems
summary_en: Humorous first-person column from the United States listing ways Bangladeshis harm their own immigration cases: a student whose visa was cancelled after posting on Facebook asking for help finding off-campus restaurant or gas-station work, a student deported after allegedly trying to forcibly kiss a woman at his gas-station job, social media posts promoting switching a visitor visa to asylum, and careless form-filling, including an applicant who wrote a date of death for living parents in an immigration petition. It also describes US hospital billing.

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi had his US student visa cancelled because, right after getting it, he posted a Facebook status asking whether any 'elder brother' could help him find restaurant or gas station work in the United States.

According to the columnist, a student in the United States is legally not supposed to work off campus (some institutions allow it); students who do such jobs do it secretly, and authorities pretend not to see unless it is made public, in which case they are forced to act.

A Bangladeshi student in one US state had his student visa cancelled and was sent back to Bangladesh, reportedly for trying to forcibly kiss an unknown woman at the gas station where he worked; his family had spent heavily, possibly selling land, to send him abroad to study, and was ruined.

The columnist warns that some Bangladeshis post on Facebook how to come to the United States on a visitor visa and switch to asylum, and share irregular ('dui nombori') routes; he says if US immigration notices such posts it will become harder for ordinary Bangladeshis to get visas.

The columnist says each of his children was born by C-section in a US hospital; mother and baby were released the same or next day, the bill each time was over USD 50,000 for two days, and he paid USD 6,000 as insurance deductible, with the rest recovered from the insurance company.

According to the columnist, US hospitals do not keep patients even an hour longer than needed because insurers will not pay for unnecessary admission; a low-income vlogger in New York had city insurance and paid nothing out of pocket.

The columnist warns that a Bangladeshi vlogger's video calling US hospitals bad (because a newborn was kept separately for three days, likely for intensive care) could make others avoid taking wives to hospital, risking deaths of mothers or babies.

A woman who applied for US immigration for her parents was told by the embassy that the parents had died in 2002, because a date had been entered in the 'date of death' field of the application; the parents then had to prove they were alive. The columnist warns not to fill in fields that do not apply (leave blank or write 'NA', not the Bangla word 'na').

headline_en: Tripartite agreement signed for online attestation of certificates of students going abroad
summary_en: On 18 February 2025 the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the University Grants Commission (UGC) and the a2i (Aspire to Innovate) programme signed an MoU at UGC to attest certificates of students going abroad online using the apostille system through the MyGov platform, with fees paid via the national payment gateway 'ekPay'. The foreign ministry will draft rules for the apostille system, UGC will instruct universities, and the foreign secretary urged extending online attestation to embassies abroad.

facts.statement: On Tuesday 18 February 2025 the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the University Grants Commission (UGC) and the Aspire to Innovate (a2i) programme signed a tripartite memorandum of understanding at UGC to make attestation of certificates for students going abroad easier, faster and safer.
Under the February 2025 agreement, students of universities under UGC can pay the certificate attestation fee for applications on the MyGov platform using the national payment gateway 'ekPay' (একপে).
facts.source_in_article: Press release; UGC chairman Prof. S M A Faiz

facts.statement: The foreign ministry, education ministry, a2i of the ICT ministry and UGC will complete attestation of certificates of students from all universities in Bangladesh who want to go abroad through apostille on the MyGov platform; this is for students seeking higher education or jobs abroad and is meant to save time, effort and money.

Under the MoU, the foreign ministry will make the rules, guidelines or policy needed to implement the apostille system and coordinate all parties; UGC will instruct universities to implement it, inform students through universities about paying the attestation management charge, and give universities access to the integrated online attestation management system.
The agreement was signed by a2i project director Md. Mamunur Rashid Bhuiyan, UGC secretary Md. Fakhrul Islam and foreign ministry Director General (Consular and Welfare) Shah Mohammad Tanvir Mansur.

Foreign secretary (East) Muhammad Nazrul Islam said bringing all universities onto one online attestation platform had been very difficult, and urged those concerned to start online certificate attestation at Bangladesh embassies abroad as well.

headline_en: Where are the 20,000 'missing' Indian students who went to Canada
summary_en: Canadian government figures published in March-April 2024 flagged about 50,000 international students as 'no-shows' who got study permits but did not start studying, including about 20,000 Indians (5.4%). Of 11,948 students from Bangladesh in the period, 7.5% did not contact their college or university. Indian media report many work to support themselves, some were cheated by fake colleges, some crossed illegally into the US, and asylum claims by foreign students hit a record in 2024. Working without a work permit is illegal in Canada.

facts.statement: According to Canadian government statistics published in March-April 2024, about 50,000 foreign students at Canadian colleges and universities were marked as 'no-show': they came with study permits but did not start studying.
facts.source_in_article: Canadian government statistics, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Of 11,948 students who went from Bangladesh to study in Canada in the period covered by the March-April 2024 figures, 7.5% did not contact their university or college after arriving in Canada, i.e. did not go there to study.
facts.source_in_article: Canadian government statistics, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: No-show rates in the Canadian figures (published March-April 2024): India about 20,000 students (5.4% of its total), Philippines 2.2%, China 6.4%, Iran 11.6%, Rwanda 48.1%.

Under Canada's International Student Compliance Regime, launched in 2014, educational institutions report twice a year whether students are attending classes in line with their study permit conditions.
In Canada it is not possible to work legally anywhere without a work permit.

Prothom Alo writes that healthcare in Canada is public, so a student working illegally who falls ill must go to public healthcare where police may catch them; it also says Canada is about to take tough action against illegal immigrants.

Indian media report that many Indian students were cheated by fake colleges in Canada: on arrival they found the institutions were fake or lacked facilities. A 24-year-old from Panchkula, Haryana thought he was admitted to a well-known college in Brampton, but the address on the admission letter was a small office with no classrooms; he was told classes were full and to wait, and after weeks realised the college was fake. He had paid INR 4.2 lakh of a 12 lakh 'tuition fee'.
facts.source_in_article: Times of India / Economic Times, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The Haryana student dealt with a student agent only by phone; after he paid INR 4 lakh, the agent assured him he could pay the rest of the fee through part-time work without extra loans. He then started working at a local petrol pump.
facts.source_in_article: Times of India, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: According to Economic Times, some Indian students deliberately misused the Canadian student visa system to enter Canada for work, exploiting the policy that tuition fees need not be paid in advance.
facts.source_in_article: Economic Times, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: A 27-year-old from Valsad, Gujarat enrolled in a community college in Canada for INR 7.5 lakh for 2 years, on average three times cheaper than a master's degree in Canada; he said many with places at good colleges have loans of 25 lakh or more. He works two jobs, at a restaurant and night food delivery.
facts.source_in_article: Times of India, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: A 26-year-old from Khammam, Telangana enrolled at a college in Surrey but never attended class; he works full time at a mobile phone shop for USD 7 per hour (as printed). A 25-year-old from Ongole, Andhra Pradesh works as a delivery agent in Toronto.
facts.source_in_article: Times of India, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Indian authorities said some students went to Canada and then entered the United States illegally; Canada has no count of how many. Student organisations say some use Canada as a gateway to enter the US illegally.

According to former federal economist and immigration expert Henry Lotin, most missing Indian students did not cross the border but are working in Canada and trying to settle; the number of foreign students claiming asylum in Canada rose to a record in 2024, and at least 10% of student visa holders were unaccounted for.
facts.source_in_article: Henry Lotin, former federal economist and immigration expert

facts.statement: Henry Lotin proposed requiring foreign students to pay full tuition before coming to Canada to reduce fake applicants. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) has contacted Indian authorities and is investigating the issue.

headline_en: 17 rescued from traffickers' hideout in Teknaf, one held
summary_en: On 25 January 2025 the Bangladesh Navy raided a human traffickers' hideout in the hills of Kachchhopia, Baharchhara union, Teknaf, Cox's Bazar, rescuing 17 people including women and children (3 Bangladeshis, the rest Rohingya camp residents) held hostage for trafficking by sea to Malaysia, and arrested trafficker Ali Abdullah. The union chairman said syndicates lure Rohingyas with promises of Malaysia, hold them in the hills and demand ransom; about 150 victims were rescued in January 2025 alone.

facts.statement: On the afternoon of Saturday 25 January 2025 the Bangladesh Navy raided a human traffickers' hideout in the hilly area of Kachchhopia, Baharchhara union, Teknaf upazila, Cox's Bazar, acting on a tip-off, and rescued 17 women, men and children held hostage to be trafficked by sea to Malaysia; trafficker Ali Abdullah was arrested.
facts.source_in_article: Lt Cdr Afzal Hossain, Bangladesh Navy Teknaf contingent

facts.statement: Of the 17 rescued in Teknaf on 25 January 2025, 3 were Bangladeshi citizens and the rest were residents of Rohingya camps in Ukhia and Teknaf.

Human traffickers operate as syndicates through several points along the coast of Baharchhara union, Teknaf, bringing Rohingyas from camps in Ukhia-Teknaf; they lure them with promises of sending them to Malaysia, hold them captive in the hills and demand ransom.
facts.source_in_article: Amjad Hossain, chairman, Baharchhara union parishad

facts.statement: About 150 or more cheated people were rescued in police, RAB and Navy operations in the Teknaf area in January 2025 alone.
facts.source_in_article: Amjad Hossain, chairman, Baharchhara union parishad

facts.statement: The Navy handed 18 people (17 rescued plus 1 trafficker) to Teknaf Model police station around 7 pm on 25 January 2025; the trafficker was to be sent to Cox's Bazar court on 26 January 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Muhammad Gias Uddin, OC, Teknaf Model police station

headline_en: We want a roadmap to end unemployment (editorial)
summary_en: Editorial questioning BBS unemployment figures (26.6 lakh unemployed in July-September 2024 under the 19th ICLS method, 25.5 lakh under the old one). It says 20 to 22 lakh people enter the job market each year but only 13 to 14 lakh find work at home, overseas job opportunities for Bangladeshi workers are shrinking, and thousands still go abroad amid great uncertainty, many ruined by brokers.

facts.statement: Every year 20 to 22 lakh people enter Bangladesh's job market, of whom 13 to 14 lakh find employment in the country, according to a January 2025 Prothom Alo editorial.

The January 2025 editorial says opportunities for Bangladeshi workers to work abroad have been shrinking recently, and that migrant workers who went abroad in '2014' (as printed; context suggests the latest year) were three lakh fewer than the previous year.

The editorial says that because there is no proper employment at home, thousands of job seekers go abroad despite great uncertainty, and many fall into the clutches of brokers (dalal) and lose everything.

According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), 26.6 lakh people were unemployed in July-September 2024 under the 19th ICLS method; under the old method the number was 25.5 lakh at end-September 2024. The labour force at end-September 2024 was 7.06 crore (4.749 crore men, 2.257 crore women) per the 13th ICLS-based quarterly survey.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics, cited in editorial

facts.statement: According to BGMEA, 100 garment factories have closed since the July-August 2024 uprising.

summary_en: Column by economist Selim Raihan on Bangladesh's economic challenges at the start of 2025: persistent inflation, foreign exchange pressure, stalled investment and labour unrest. It says exports and remittance have given some hope and improved reserves, and recommends digital banking, mobile financial services, incentive packages for expatriates and strengthening the expatriate welfare fund to increase legal-channel remittance.

facts.statement: Selim Raihan wrote in January 2025 that remittance inflows had recently played an important role in increasing Bangladesh's foreign exchange reserves.
facts.source_in_article: Selim Raihan, professor of economics, Dhaka University, and executive director, SANEM (column)

headline_en: High commission to open in New Zealand; notification to declare Kazi Nazrul 'national poet'
summary_en: On 5 December 2024 the interim government's advisory council approved setting up a Bangladesh High Commission in Wellington, New Zealand. The Cabinet Division said about 10,000 Bangladeshis live in New Zealand and about 1,000 Bangladeshi students study there, and that consular services from Australia (the concurrently accredited mission) cannot always reach them, forcing costly trips to Australia; costs will be met in FY2025-26.

facts.statement: On Thursday 5 December 2024 the interim government's advisory council, chaired by Chief Adviser Dr Muhammad Yunus, approved establishing a Bangladesh High Commission in Wellington, New Zealand; all expenses will be met in the next fiscal year (2025-26).
About 10,000 Bangladeshis live in New Zealand and about 1,000 Bangladeshi students study at universities there.

Bangladeshis in New Zealand have been served by the Bangladesh mission in Australia, which is concurrently accredited; proper service from Australia is not always possible, and expatriates face high costs and other difficulties travelling to Australia for consular services.
The Cabinet Division said that once the Wellington high commission is set up, all kinds of consular services will reach Bangladeshis in New Zealand directly, more easily and cheaply.
72 countries, including India and Pakistan, have diplomatic missions in New Zealand; New Zealand ranks 16th on the Human Development Index and 32nd on the global competitiveness index.

headline_en: Preparing to study abroad? Are you making these 5 mistakes
summary_en: Lifestyle feature listing five misconceptions among Bangladeshis planning to study abroad: that IELTS/TOEFL is unnecessary, that shortcuts via agencies or fake certificates work, that one can enrol in one country and move to another, that scholarships cover all costs, and that studying abroad brings citizenship and jobs. Bangladeshi students abroad warn against advertisements promising study abroad for BDT 10 lakh, offer letters from places like Cyprus, and note limits on off-campus work in the US and language needs for jobs in Germany and the Netherlands.

facts.statement: Without IELTS or TOEFL it is almost impossible to go to study in the United States, Canada or various European countries; Atanu Chakraborty (doctoral student, College of Pharmacy, University of Iowa) said the scores matter for admission and also for the visa, as most embassies and visa authorities assess applications based on them, and advised avoiding institutions that invite students abroad without these scores.
facts.source_in_article: Atanu Chakraborty, doctoral student, University of Iowa

facts.statement: Some students believe they can prepare papers in a few weeks, submit fake certificates and get a study visa, or that an agency will do all the paperwork; the article says this is not possible and taking a 'shortcut' carries a high risk of trouble later.

Mohidul Alam (student, New York University) warned not to fall for flashy advertisements such as 'go to study abroad by spending BDT 10 lakh'; he advised verifying information, starting preparation (IELTS/TOEFL, GRE) from after the HSC exam, and emailing foreign universities' admission offices directly rather than always using an agency.
facts.source_in_article: Mohidul Alam, student, New York University

facts.statement: Mohidul Alam said some students reach a foreign country to find no place to live and no work, and that money is needed to cover at least the first few months.

According to the article, under most scholarship and visa conditions students must return home after finishing their studies; opportunities to take citizenship or move to another country are limited, and course or credit transfer is rarely possible.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo; Rounak Saha, PhD student, UNSW

facts.statement: Rounak Saha (PhD student, University of New South Wales, Australia) warned against enrolling in a little-known European country or university planning to move later to another country, and said many come abroad with offer letters from countries including Cyprus and risk losing money and being cheated in various ways.
Most scholarships cover only tuition fees; living, travel and other costs are usually borne by the student, and it is hard to meet all costs without part-time work, which may be limited.
Rounak Saha said opportunities to work off campus are limited in the United States, while Australia offers some opportunity.
Rounak Saha said in countries such as Germany or the Netherlands you need to know the local language to get jobs or part-time work while studying; without it opportunities are very limited.

G M Majidul Islam (student, Central Queensland University) said studying abroad does not guarantee citizenship, which requires separate eligibility and conditions, and that part-time work is bound by many rules; breaking the law can bring fines and other trouble.
facts.source_in_article: G M Majidul Islam, student, Central Queensland University

facts.statement: Anika Tabassum (graduate, Queen Mary University of London) said the work environment abroad is challenging, many fall ill from unprepared exposure to the weather in Europe or America, and students planning to come with family or a spouse should plan carefully.
facts.source_in_article: Anika Tabassum, Queen Mary University of London
